explanations.explanation: Luke 4:15 says He taught in their synagogues and “…was glorified by everyone.” Everyone, friend. I can't even get a whole family to agree on one cookie shape, so that's a big deal.

No one walks out in this verse. It says He taught in their synagogues and was glorified by everyone. I've watched people leave a kitchen when the dough ran out, but this is nothing like that. The people here are praising Him.

Luke 4:15 doesn't say anything about empty rooms. The news about Him had spread through the region (Luke 4:14), and He was glorified by everyone. An empty room is a lonely thing, and I know that feeling from my drawer days. This isn't that.
Luke 4:16 says it plainly: “Then Jesus came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up.” This is His hometown. Everybody in that town has known Him a long time, and that matters for what comes next.

Bethlehem is where Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1), so I see why it came to mind. But Luke 4:16 asks about the town where He was brought up, and that's Nazareth. Born in one place and raised in another, just like plenty of folks you know.

Bethany was the village of Mary and Martha (John 11:1), so it's a real place with real friends of Jesus in it. It's just not the one in this passage. Luke 4:16 names Nazareth as the town where He was brought up.

Luke 4:16 says, “As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath.” That word custom means it's a habit, not a one-time visit. Some people have a favorite chair at church. Jesus has a routine here too.

The text says the opposite. Luke 4:16 reads, “As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath.” So going in on the Sabbath is what He usually does. It's a habit of His, not a surprise visit.

Luke 4:17 says “the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to Him.” Isaiah was a prophet of God. Jesus unrolls the scroll and finds the exact place He wants. No searching around like I do for the right mixing bowl.
Jeremiah is a real prophet, and people even guessed Jesus might be him (Matthew 16:14). But he isn't the one in this passage. The scroll handed to Jesus in Luke 4:17 belongs to the prophet Isaiah.
Daniel is a prophet too (Matthew 24:15). Good name, friend, but he's not the one here. Luke 4:17 says the scroll handed to Jesus is the scroll of the prophet Isaiah.

The reading says He has sent Me to proclaim “…recovery of sight to the blind.” That's right there in Luke 4:18. The poor get good news, and the blind get sight back. That list is longer than my cookie order on a holiday.

The rich aren't on the list in the reading. In Luke 4:18 the speaker is sent to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim liberty to the captives, to give recovery of sight to the blind, and to release the oppressed. The blind are the ones named on this card.
The mighty aren't named in this reading. Luke 4:18 lists the poor, the captives, the blind and the oppressed. Of those, the blind are the ones on this card. Keep an eye on that list, friend.

The text says the opposite. Luke 4:20 says, “The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him.” Nobody is looking away or going back to their own business. You could hear a pin drop in there. I bet you could hear a cookie crumb drop.
Luke 4:20 says, “The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on Him.” Everyone is watching, not wandering off. I think a room that quiet is waiting to hear what He says next.
He begins by saying, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.” (Luke 4:21) Today, right there in the room. He doesn't say it's coming later. He says this is happening while they listen.
Jesus doesn't push it off to someday. Luke 4:21 has Him say, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.” The word is today. Nobody in that room has to wait.

That's not what He says. He tells the people, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.” (Luke 4:21) He doesn't talk about Isaiah's life at all. He talks about today, and about what they just heard.

The crowd asks, “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?” (Luke 4:22) They're talking about Joseph as someone they know. I think they're trying to figure out how the local guy got so impressive. People do that at family reunions all the time.
Zebedee was the father of James and John (Matthew 4:21), so he's a real name from Jesus' story. But it's not the one the crowd uses. In Luke 4:22 they ask, “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?”
Jesse was King David's father (1 Samuel 17:12), so that's a good Bible name to have in your pocket. But the crowd in Nazareth doesn't use it. In Luke 4:22 they ask, “Isn’t this the son of Joseph?”
Jesus says they'll tell Him, “Do here in Your hometown what we have heard that You did in Capernaum.” (Luke 4:23) Capernaum is where they heard He did things. They want to see it in person.
Jericho isn't mentioned in this passage. In Luke 4:23 Jesus says they'll point to what they heard He did in Capernaum. That's the town the crowd names.
Hebron doesn't show up in this passage. The town the crowd has heard about is Capernaum, in Luke 4:23. They'd like to see those same things in Nazareth.

Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in his hometown.” (Luke 4:24) A prophet can be known and loved in one place and still not accepted at home. I think that stings. Home is where you want a good reception.
Jesus says the opposite. In Luke 4:24 He says, “Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in his hometown.” Hometown is where it's hardest, not where he's honored most.

explanations.answer: He must never go back there
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that, and He's standing in His own hometown as He says this. Luke 4:24 reads, “Truly I tell you, no prophet is accepted in his hometown.” That's about acceptance. It's not a rule about staying away.

Jesus says the opposite. Luke 4:26 reads, “Yet Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon.” There were many widows in Israel, but Elijah was sent to none of them. That one can trip you up.
Jesus says, “Yet Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon.” (Luke 4:26) Many widows in Israel, and Elijah wasn't sent to any of them. He was sent somewhere else.
Jesus says Elijah was sent “…to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon.” (Luke 4:26) So he wasn't sent to a widow in Israel at all. Zarephath in Sidon is where he was sent.
Nineveh was a great city (Jonah 1:2), and it's a real Bible place. But it's not where Elijah was sent. Luke 4:26 says he was sent to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon.
Tarsus in Cilicia is where Paul said he was from (Acts 21:39), so it's a real Bible place. But Elijah isn't sent there. Luke 4:26 says he was sent to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon.

Jesus says there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha's time, “Yet not one of them was cleansed—only Naaman the Syrian.” (Luke 4:27) Naaman is the one named in this verse. Many lepers, one cleansed, and he came from outside Israel.
Hazael became king after Ben-hadad (2 Kings 8:15), so he's a Bible name. But Jesus doesn't use it here. In Luke 4:27 the one cleansed is Naaman the Syrian.
Ben-hadad was a king of Aram (2 Kings 8:7), so you picked a name from Bible history. But it's not the one in this verse. In Luke 4:27 the one cleansed is Naaman the Syrian.
Luke 4:28 says, “On hearing this, all the people in the synagogue were enraged.” All of them. It's a heavy turn, and a sudden one. A moment ago they were speaking well of Him.
The text says otherwise. Luke 4:28 reads, “On hearing this, all the people in the synagogue were enraged.” That's everyone in the room, not just a few. It's a heavy moment, friend.

explanations.answer: To throw Him over the cliff
explanations.explanation: Luke 4:29 says they led Him to the brow of the hill “…in order to throw Him over the cliff.” It's a hard thing to read, and I think it hurts. It's the same crowd from just a few verses earlier.

The text gives a very different reason. Luke 4:29 says they drove Him out of the town and led Him to the brow of the hill “…in order to throw Him over the cliff.” This isn't a teaching trip. It's a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: To show Him the whole region
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says. In Luke 4:29 they drive Him out and lead Him to the brow of the hill “…in order to throw Him over the cliff.” It's a hard line to read.
The text says otherwise. Luke 4:30 reads, “But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way.” They never throw Him over. He walks right through them and goes on.
Luke 4:30 says, “But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way.” They led Him to the edge to throw Him, but they don't do it. He passes through the crowd and keeps going.
